Summary
Engineered filamentous phage nanofibers have been used as programmable scaffolds to present peptides that capture clinically relevant cervical biomarkers with higher assay sensitivity than conventional antibody-only ELISA, supporting dual- and multiplexed diagnostics and offering a scalable, manufacturable platform for point‑of‑care applications. <cite id="c367735c-1">Engineered fd phage nanofibers displaying peptides that bind VEGF and PD‑L1 enabled simultaneous detection of both proteins in a single ELISA assay and improved diagnostic accuracy versus conventional ELISA</cite>. <cite id="c367735c-2">In serum from cervical cancer patients, dual‑display phage nanofibers raised positive rates compared to single‑target antibodies and yielded higher AUCs (0.896 vs 0.826) and significantly higher sensitivity and specificity</cite>. <cite id="c367735c-3">As a class, nanofibers offer high surface area, loading capacity, and enhanced stability/activity of immobilized biomolecules, enabling highly sensitive and selective biosensors and explaining the performance gains observed with engineered fd phage nanofibers</cite>. <cite id="c367735c-4">A generalizable strategy of combining phage nanofiber capture with antigen co‑capture (e.g., p53) boosted detection rates and accuracy in cancer patients, supporting dual‑modal capture for biomarker‑antibody interactions</cite>.

Biomarker landscape for cervical cancer
Cervical cancer detection benefits from multiple biomarker modalities spanning viral nucleic acids (E6/E7 mRNA, HPV DNA), viral oncoproteins/antibodies, and host tumor proteins. <cite id="a951530b-0">Ultrasensitive ELISA quantification of HPV16 E7 oncoprotein in urine detected attomolar concentrations and discriminated oncogenic activity, revealing discrepancies versus E6/E7 PCR DNA presence, consistent with differences in viral life‑cycle and oncogenic activity</cite>. <cite id="a951530b-2">The ELISA distinguished specimens with low or no E7 from PCR‑positive ones, suggesting inactive infection; the assay related E7 levels to CIN grade and showed specificity for HPV16/related types over HPV18</cite>. <cite id="a951530b-1">A systematic review/meta‑analysis concluded that HPV16/18 E6/E7 antibodies show high specificity but suboptimal sensitivity for cervical cancer/CIN3 detection, supporting their utility as adjunct biomarkers but not as stand‑alone screening tools at present</cite>. <cite id="a951530b-3">HPV E6/E7 mRNA assays can outperform DNA genotyping for specificity and relate to lesion severity, yet E6/E7 mRNA positivity is lower in intraepithelial lesions and higher in carcinomas, implying value for triage and prognosis</cite>. <cite id="a951530b-4">A multiplex electrochemiluminescence immunoassay quantified type‑specific IgG to HPV16/18 E6 and E7, enabling analyte‑wise reference assignment and demonstrating assay specificity via competition/cross‑reactivity analyses</cite>.

Engineered filamentous phage nanofibers: materials, display, and design principles
Filamentous phage (e.g., M13/fd) provide biocompatible, high‑aspect‑ratio nanofibers that can be genetically programmed to display multiple targeting peptides and host affinity reagents or antigens. <cite id="c367735c-1">A dual‑display fd phage was engineered to present peptides that bind VEGF and PD‑L1; the nanofiber served as a capture reagent in ELISA and exhibited enhanced detection sensitivity versus single‑target antibody capture</cite>. <cite id="c367735c-2">In sandwich phage‑ELISA, phage nanoparticles at 50 μg/mL as coating showed positive serum rates of 78.9% for VEGF/sPD‑L1 versus 49.3% and 52.1% for single markers; AUCs improved from 0.756–0.778 to 0.896 when phage nanofibers were used as capture probes, with significantly higher sensitivity and specificity</cite>. <cite id="c367735c-3">Nanofiber architecture improves immobilization capacity and activity/stability of attached biomolecules, and fd phage nanofibers equipped with peptide fragments have been applied to cervical biomarker detection with higher sensitivity than conventional ELISA</cite>. <cite id="c367735c-4">Beyond peptide capture alone, combining phage nanofibers with co‑captured antigens (e.g., p53) synergistically increased detection rates and diagnostic accuracy in mixed cancer cohorts, illustrating modular “dual capture” engineering that can be transported to cervical markers</cite>.

Design takeaways include multivalency and orientation: multiple peptides can be arrayed along the nanofiber to increase local concentration and avidity, while the virus capsid provides structural context and stability. <cite id="c367735c-1">Dual peptide display on a single phage backbone enabled simultaneous recognition and binding of two biomarkers in one format, reducing assay complexity and enabling multiplexing</cite>. <cite id="c367735c-3">High surface area and loading capacity facilitate dense immobilization of capture elements or enzyme labels, improving signal and enabling integration with amplification strategies</cite>.

Assay platforms and performance with phage nanofibers
- Sandwich ELISA with phage nanofiber capture. <cite id="c367735c-1">Engineered dual‑peptide fd phage nanofibers captured VEGF and sPD‑L1 in a single ELISA, outperforming conventional antibody capture for each biomarker</cite>. <cite id="c367735c-2">Clinical serum testing showed 78.9% positive rate with phage nanofibers versus 49.3% and 52.1% with single‑target antibodies; AUCs improved from 0.756–0.778 to 0.896 and sensitivity/specificity were significantly higher (P<0.01)</cite>. <cite id="c367735c-1">The method supports single‑target or multiplex detection within one well, offering flexibility for prognostic panels (e.g., VEGF + PDL‑1) relevant to therapy response and progression</cite>.
- Electrochemical and nucleic acid biosensors (modality expansion). While not phage display per se, these establish performance baselines and integration routes compatible with phage nanofiber scaffolds. <cite id="efa460c7-0">HR‑HPV nucleic acid biosensors using isothermal amplification and CRISPR combine with lateral flow/electrochemical readouts to deliver portable, high‑sensitivity HPV testing suitable for point‑of‑care</cite>. <cite id="efa460c7-1">A duplex electrochemical gene biosensor detected HPV16 E2 and E6 at 8 and 12 copies/mL, discriminated episomal vs integrated HPV forms via E2/E6 ratio (cut‑off 0.77, 100% sensitivity/specificity), and matched qPCR on 30 clinical tissues</cite>. <cite id="efa460c7-2">A multianalyte electrochemical genosensor achieved 20–22 fM LODs for HPV16/18 with clinical sample consistency to nested PCR, completing assays in 90 minutes</cite>. <cite id="efa460c7-3">Electrochemical HPV16 E6/E7 mRNA biosensors with signal amplification reached detection limits around 0.08 fM (~100 copies), leveraging gold nanoparticles, RT‑LAMP, and biotin–streptavidin; paper‑based electrochemical sensors integrated PNA probes and graphene‑polypyrrole electrodes for HPV16 DNA</cite>. <cite id="efa460c7-4">Electrochemical biosensors for cervical biomarkers offer higher sensitivity, affordability, and ease of analysis compared to traditional cytology, with reviews synthesizing biomarker panels and platform limitations/future directions</cite>.
- Serological/oncoprotein assays and phage‑based capture. <cite id="a951530b-0">E7 oncoprotein ELISA in urine achieved attomolar detection and related E7 levels to CIN grade, highlighting protein‑based readouts that could be adapted to phage nanofiber architectures</cite>. <cite id="c367735c-4">Phage nanofiber capture of anti‑p53 antibodies plus antigen co‑capture yielded detection rates of 30.4% in 316 cancer patients and the highest diagnostic accuracy, illustrating a transferable design pattern for phage cervical biosensors targeting human antibodies to tumor antigens</cite>.
- General biomaterials support. <cite id="c367735c-3">Nanofiber platforms enhance immobilization capacity and biomolecule activity/stability; engineered fd phage peptide‑display systems have already been applied to cervical biomarker detection with sensitivity exceeding traditional ELISA</cite>.

Advantages and limitations relative to conventional diagnostics
Advantages:
- Sensitivity and multiplexing via multivalent peptide display and dense immobilization. <cite id="c367735c-2">Phage nanofiber capture raised positive rates and AUCs versus single‑target antibody capture and conventional ELISA, with significantly higher sensitivity and specificity in patient serum</cite>. <cite id="c367735c-1">Single assay panels (e.g., VEGF + sPD‑L1) provide prognostic and therapeutic value</cite>. <cite id="c367735c-3">High surface area and loading capacity improve capture density and stability, enabling robust signals and integration with amplification labels</cite>.
- Scalable, manufacturable capture scaffolds. <cite id="c367735c-1">Phage nanofibers can be mass‑produced via bacterial infection and genetically engineered for specific peptide displays, supporting cost‑effective probe fabrication</cite>. <cite id="c367735c-4">The combination of phage nanofibers and antigens provides a modular “dual capture” unit applicable across tumor markers</cite>.
- Complementary readouts to HPV DNA and cytology. <cite id="a951530b-0">Protein‑based E7 assays distinguish active oncogenesis from DNA persistence, addressing limitations of DNA positivity in transient infections</cite>. <cite id="efa460c7-3">Electrochemical mRNA genotyping achieves femtomolar LODs and rapid cycles, offering a bridge between molecular PCR gold standards and accessible POC formats</cite>.

Limitations and considerations:
- Specificity and sensitivity trade‑offs for serological markers. <cite id="a951530b-1">HPV antibody and E6/E7 protein serological markers show high specificity but suboptimal sensitivity for cervical cancer/CIN3, suggesting cautious use as adjuncts rather than stand‑alone tests until further validation</cite>.
- Matrix effects, biofouling, and assay interference. <cite id="c367735c-3">Although nanofibers enhance biomolecule activity and lifetime, performance depends on surface chemistry, orientation, and loading; optimization is required to minimize non‑specific binding and maximize selectivity</cite>.
- Standardization and regulatory translation. <cite id="efa460c7-0">HR‑HPV biosensors show promise for POC, but face challenges in cost and reproducibility; similar considerations likely apply to phage‑based platforms at scale, necessitating rigorous quality control and validation</cite>.
- Corroboration with primary modalities. <cite id="a951530b-0">Protein and DNA readouts can diverge due to viral life‑cycle dynamics; integrating phage‑based protein assays with HPV DNA/E6/E7 mRNA genotyping can improve risk stratification</cite>. <cite id="efa460c7-1">Electrochemical gene sensors can mirror qPCR performance on clinical tissues, supporting a tiered workflow where phage‑based protein panels inform prognosis and therapy selection</cite>.

Practical deployment: workflows and clinical integration
A practical strategy is to combine HPV molecular genotyping (HPV DNA/E6/E7 mRNA) with phage‑nanofiber ELISA panels for tumor microenvironment proteins (e.g., VEGF, PD‑L1, p16/INK4a, cytokeratins, HE4) to stratify risk, prognosis, and therapy response. <cite id="c367735c-1">VEGF and sPD‑L1 jointly improved diagnostic value over single markers, aligning with clinical rationales for anti‑VEGF/PD‑(L)1 strategies</cite>. <cite id="c367735c-2">Phage‑ELISA achieved higher diagnostic accuracy than conventional ELISA for the same biomarkers, supporting adoption as a sensitive complement to molecular testing</cite>. <cite id="efa460c7-3">Electrochemical HPV mRNA biosensors with femtomolar LODs and rapid turnaround can underpin POC triage, while phage ELISAs offer centralized or fieldable multiplex panels for prognosis and monitoring</cite>. <cite id="a951530b-1">Given current sensitivity limits of serological oncoprotein/antibody markers, phage‑based assays should be integrated as adjuncts with HPV DNA and cytology, particularly for triage of HPV‑positive or CIN2+/3+ cohorts</cite>.

Engineering roadmap and future directions
- Expand peptide/phage display libraries and valency/spacing optimization for HPV proteins (E6, E7), host antibodies (e.g., anti‑p16), and extracellular vesicle/lipid markers; integrate antigen co‑capture to boost weakly expressed targets. <cite id="c367735c-1">Dual peptide display on a single nanofiber demonstrates parallel multiplexing within one well</cite>. <cite id="c367735c-4">Phage + antigen dual capture raised detection rates and accuracy for anti‑p53; the same pattern can be applied to cervical tumor antigens</cite>.
- Move beyond ELISA: leverage phage nanofibers as building blocks for electrochemical immunosensors, SERS substrates, and paper‑based lateral flow via covalent coupling to electrodes and nanoparticle labels, borrowing from high‑performance nucleic acid sensors. <cite id="efa460c7-1">Electrochemical gene biosensors can detect HPV E2/E6 at 8–12 copies/mL with 100% sensitivity/specificity on clinical tissues</cite>. <cite id="efa460c7-2">Electrochemical genosensors achieved 20–22 fM LODs for HPV16/18 with clinical sample consistency</cite>. <cite id="efa460c7-3">Electrochemical HPV mRNA assays reach ~0.08 fM LOD using RT‑LAMP and AuNP/PNA architectures</cite>.
- Clinical validation and standardization: establish external quality assessment across serum/urine/tissue matrices; compare head‑to‑head with Hybrid Capture/PCR/cytology; implement standardized peptide coupling and phage coating protocols to ensure reproducibility and cost control. <cite id="efa460c7-0">HR‑HPV biosensors show promise but face reproducibility/cost challenges; phage platforms should address these to enable POC</cite>. <cite id="c367735c-2">Demonstrated gains over conventional ELISA on patient serum support further validation on larger cohorts and across specimen types</cite>.
- Theranostics and monitoring: pair phage‑nanofiber diagnostics with aptamer/enzyme reporters and smartphone readouts for home or clinic use; integrate with HPV vaccine/therapy monitoring by tracking anti‑E6/E7/p16 dynamics and immune checkpoints like PD‑(L)1. <cite id="c367735c-1">VEGF and sPD‑L1 measurements inform therapy response and prognosis, supporting immunotherapy drug development</cite>. <cite id="efa460c7-4">Electrochemical readouts are affordable and sensitive, enabling scalable deployment for early detection and monitoring</cite>.

Key takeaways for advanced detection
- Biomarker selection should combine viral markers (HPV16/18 DNA, E6/E7 mRNA) with host tumor/oncologic proteins and immune checkpoints to capture carcinogenic activity and therapeutic targets. <cite id="a951530b-0">E7 protein ELISA distinguishes active oncogenesis from DNA persistence and correlates with CIN grade</cite>. <cite id="a951530b-3">E6/E7 mRNA outperforms DNA for specificity and relates to lesion severity</cite>. <cite id="c367735c-1">VEGF and PD‑L1 jointly improve diagnostic/prognostic value</cite>.
- Filamentous phage nanofibers offer a unique materials platform: genetically programmable peptide display, high surface area and loading capacity, and mass production enable sensitive, multiplexed capture formats with performance exceeding conventional ELISA. <cite id="c367735c-2">Phage‑ELISA achieved higher positive rates and AUCs than conventional ELISA for VEGF and sPD‑L1 in cervical cancer patients</cite>. <cite id="c367735c-3">Nanofiber properties enhance biomolecule activity/stability and loading, and engineered fd phage peptide‑display systems have already demonstrated higher sensitivity than traditional ELISA for cervical biomarker detection</cite>.
- Translation requires integrating phage‑based protein panels with approved HPV molecular tests, moving from bench to POC via electrochemical and lateral flow formats, while addressing specificity, biofouling, and reproducibility through surface chemistry and standardized manufacturing. <cite id="a951530b-1">Serological HPV oncoprotein/antibody markers need further optimization for sensitivity to serve as adjuncts</cite>. <cite id="efa460c7-0">HR‑HPV biosensors are well positioned for POC if cost/reproducibility hurdles are addressed</cite>.

Gaps and outlook
Direct examples of phage nanofibers in SERS/lateral flow specifically for cervical cancer are limited in the retrieved literature; however, the demonstrated ELISA gains and compatibility with electrochemical genosensor chemistries suggest clear pathways to POC implementation. <cite id="c367735c-1">Dual‑peptide phage ELISA with improved sensitivity and multiplexing</cite>, <cite id="c367735c-2">higher AUCs and sensitivity/specificity in patient serum</cite>, and <cite id="efa460c7-3">electrochemical HPV mRNA biosensors achieving femtomolar LODs with rapid cycles and clinical concordance to qPCR</cite> collectively support a translational trajectory. Prioritizing head‑to‑head clinical comparisons against HPV DNA/E6/E7 mRNA and cytology/colposcopy, optimizing anti‑fouling and orientation on phage nanofibers, and adopting modular “dual capture” designs for low‑abundance markers will accelerate regulatory approval and clinical adoption. <cite id="a951530b-0">E7 protein–DNA discordance underscores the value of multi‑modality assays</cite>, and <cite id="efa460c7-3">electrochemical amplification strategies provide ready‑to‑transfer toolkits for integrating phage nanofiber capture with portable detection</cite>.

Title: Advanced detection of cervical cancer biomarkers using engineered filamentous phage nanofibers
Snippet: Abstract Cervical cancer is a major global health concern, characterized by its high incidence and mortality rates. The detection of tumor markers is crucial for managing cancer, making treatment decisions, and monitoring disease progression. Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and programmed death-ligand 1 (PDL-1) are key targets in cervical cancer therapy and valuable biomarkers in predicting treatment response and prognosis. In this study, we found that combining the measurement of VEGF and soluble PDL-1 can be used for diagnosing and evaluating the progression of cervical cancer. To explore a more convenient approach for detecting and assessing cervical cancer, we designed and prepared an engineered fd bacteriophage, a human-safe viral nanofiber, equipped with two peptides targeting VEGF and PD-L1. The dual-display phage nanofiber specifically recognizes and binds to both proteins. Utilizing this nanofiber as a novel capture agent, we developed a new enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) method. This method shows significantly enhanced detection sensitivity compared to conventional ELISA methods, which use either anti-VEGF or anti-PD-L1 antibodies as capture agents. Therefore, the phage dual-display nanofiber presents significant potential in detecting cancer markers, evaluating medication efficacy, and advancing immunotherapy drug development. Key points • The combined measurement of VEGF and soluble Programmed Death-Ligand 1(sPD-L1) demonstrates an additive effect in the diagnosis of cervical cancer. Fd phage nanofibers have been ingeniously engineered to display peptides that bind to VEGF and PD-L1, enabling the simultaneous detection of both proteins within a single assay • Genetically engineered phage nanofibers, adorned with two distinct peptides, can be utilized for the diagnosis and prognosis of cancer and can be mass-produced cost-effectively through bacterial infections • Employing dual-display fd phage nanofibers as capture probes, the phage ELISA method exhibited significantly enhanced detection sensitivity compared to traditional sandwich ELISA. Furthermore, phage ELISA facilitates the detection of a single protein or the simultaneous detection of multiple proteins, rendering them powerful tools for protein analysis and diagnosis across various fields, including cancer research Graphical Abstract

Title: Advanced detection of cervical cancer biomarkers using engineered filamentous phage nanofibers
Snippet: In the sandwich phage ELISA assay, phage nanoparticles at a concentration of 50 μg/mL were employed as the coating agent. A mixture of anti-VEGF and anti-PD-L1 antibodies served as the detection antibodies. The phage nanofibers detected VEGF and sPD-L1 in serum samples with a positive rate of 78.9%. When anti-VEGF or anti-PD-L1 antibodies were used individually as detection antibodies, the positive rates for detecting VEGF alone and sPD-L1 alone in serum samples were 49.3% and 52.1%, respectively, with AUC values of 0.756 and 0.778 (P < 0.01) (refer to Fig. S1 and Fig. S2). In comparison, using anti-VEGF or anti-PD-L1 antibodies alone as the coating agent resulted in only 42.3% and 49.3% of serum samples testing positive for each biomarker, respectively. This suggests that the fd phage nanofibers displaying peptides enhanced detection efficiency of biomarkers in cervical cancer patients. The AUC for serum VEGF and sPD-L1 was 0.896 when employing the phage ELISA method (Fig. 5), compared to 0.826 when using a combined measurement approach in the conventional sandwich ELISA method. This demonstrates the phage ELISA method's strong diagnostic accuracy for cervical cancer biomarkers. Additionally, a significant difference was observed between the phage ELISA and conventional ELISA methods, with the phage ELISA method exhibiting higher sensitivity and specificity (P < 0.01). 

Overall, this study demonstrated that the phage ELISA method, employing dual-display fd nanofibers as a capture probe, represents a more sensitive and efficient approach for detecting VEGF and sPD-L1 in cervical cancer patients. ROC curve analysis further substantiated the diagnostic accuracy of this method.
</snippet>

Title: Biomaterials for biomarker imaging and detection
Snippet: Characterized by high specific surface area, porosity, and high loading capacity, nanofibers are particularly useful for immobilizing recognition elements, directly interacting with target analytes, enhancing antibody immobilization, and improvi ng the activity and lifetime of biomolecules [162]. These advantages enable the development of nanofiber-based biosensors for the highly sensitive and selective detection of major disease biomarkers. Currently, the application of electrostatically spun nanofiber biosensors in biomarker detection has been extensively studied, demonstrating their capability for detecting and analyzing various disease biomarkers, including those related to cancer, CVD, and neurological disorders [162]. Additionally, nanofibers have been employed to enhance the stability and activity of enzymes, which is critical for sensitive biomarker detection. For instance, Chenafa et al. immobilized b -galactosidase in polystyrene electrospun nanofiber membranes incorporating functionalized graphene oxide, resulting in significantly improved adsorption capacity, stability, and activity of the enzyme [163]. This technique can be extended to the detection of other enzymes and biomarkers, offering new possibilities for biomedical diagnosis. Notably, Zhou et al. utilized engineered fd phage nanofibers-safe viral nanofibers equipped with peptide fragments that target specific biomarkers-for the detection of cervical cancer biomarkers [164]. This approach demonstrated higher sensitivity than the traditional ELISA method, providing new ideas and methodologies for the diagnosis and treatment of cervical cancer. 

Carbon nanotube. Carbon nanotube (CNT) has demonstrated significant potential in biomarker detection due to their outstanding electronic, structural, and optical properties [165]. The common types of CNT include SWCNTs [166], Multi-Walled Carbon Nanotubes (MWCNTs) [167], Few-Walled Carbon Nanotubes [168], and Double-Walled Carbon Nanotubes [169]. Among these, SWCNTs and MWCNTs are primarily utilized in electrochemical and electrical applications [170] (Fig. 7D).

Title: Nontoxic virus nanofibers improve the detection sensitivity for the anti-p53 antibody, a biomarker in cancer patients
Snippet: The presence of anti-p53 antibody in serum is a biomarker for cancer. However, its high sensitivity detection is still an issue in cancer diagnosis. To tackle this challenge, we used fd phage, a human-safe bacteria-specific virus nanofiber that can be mass-produced by infecting host bacteria in an error-free manner, and genetically engineered it to display a peptide capable of recognizing and capturing anti-p53 antibody on its side wall. We employed the resultant phage nanofibers as a capture probe to develop a modified version of the enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) method, termed phage-ELISA. We compared it to the traditional ELISA method for the detection of anti-p53 antibody, p53-ELISA, which uses recombinant wild-type p53 protein to capture anti-p53 antibody. We applied phage-ELISA to detect anti-p53 antibody in an experimental group of 316 patients with various types of malignant tumors. We found that a detection rate of 17.7% (56 positive cases) was achieved by phage-ELISA, which was comparable to the detection rate of 20.6% for p53-ELISA (65 positive cases). However, when both phage and p53 were combined to form antibody-capturing probes for phage/p53-ELISA, a detection rate of 30.4% (96 positive cases) was achieved. Our work showed that owing to the combined capture of the anti-p53 antibody by both phage nanofibers and p53, the phage/p53-ELISA achieved the highest diagnostic accuracy and detection efficiency for the anti-p53 antibody in patients with various types of cancers. Our work suggests that a combination of nanofibers and antigens, both of which capture antibody, could lead to increased detection sensitivity, which is useful for applications in the life sciences, clinical medicine, and environmental sciences.

Title: Portable, and ultrasensitive HR-HPV tests based on nucleic acid biosensors
Snippet: Cervical cancer is the third most common cancer threatening women’s health globally, and high-risk human papillomavirus (HR-HPV) infection is the main cause of cervical cancer worldwide. Given the recurrent nature of HR-HPV infection, accurate screening is essential for its control. Since the commonly used polymerase chain reaction (PCR) technique is limited by professional equipment and personnel, convenient and ultrasensitive detection methods for HR-HPV are still highly needed. As new molecular detection methods, nucleic acid amplification-based biosensors have the advantages of high sensitivity, rapid operation, and portability, which are helpful for point-of-care testing in rural and remote areas. This review summarized nucleic acid biosensors for HR-HPV screening based on a variety of nucleic acid amplification strategies involved in improved PCR, loop-mediated isothermal amplification, recombinase polymerase amplification, hybridization chain reaction, catalyzed hairpin assembly, and CRISPR/Cas systems. In combination with microfluidic technology, lateral flow assays, electrochemical analysis and other sensing technologies, HR-HPV nucleic acid biosensors have the advantages of high throughput, short response time, high sensitivity and easy operation in the field. Although there are still shortcomings, such as high cost and poor reproducibility, this approach will be suitable for on-site screening of HR-HPV infection or cervical cancer and for auxiliary clinical diagnosis in complex environments and poor areas in the future.
</snippet>

Title: Electrochemical Duplex Detection of E2 and E6 Genes of Human Papillomavirus Type 16 and Determination of Physical Status in High‐Risk Cervical Carcinoma
Snippet: Human papillomavirus type 16 (HPV‐16) is a key driver in the development of cervical carcinoma, with the integration of its genome into the host DNA marking a critical step in disease progression. Monitoring the physical state of HPV‐16, particularly the transition from episomal to integrated forms, is essential for evaluating the risk of malignancy development in cervix. This study presents the development of a duplex electrochemical biosensor for the simultaneous detection of the E2 and E6 genes of HPV‐16. Using a one‐step sandwich hybridization assay, the biosensor was able to detect HPV‐16 E2 and E6 genes with a sensitivity of 8 copies/mL and 12 copies/mL respectively and distinguish between the episomal and integrated forms based on the E2/E6 ratio (cut‐off 0.77, 100% sensitivity/specificity). The sensor was validated with 30 clinical cervical tissue samples, providing results comparable to qPCR method. This novel biosensor offers a rapid and efficient platform for the detection and monitoring of HPV‐16, with potential applications in cervical cancer screening and prognosis.
</snippet>

Title: A Multianalyte Electrochemical Genosensor for the Detection of High-Risk HPV Genotypes in Oral and Cervical Cancers
Snippet: Infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) is a major risk factor for oral and cervical cancers. Hence, we developed a multianalyte electrochemical DNA biosensor that could be used for both oral and cervical samples to detect the high-risk HPV genotypes 16 and 18. The assay involves the sandwich hybridization of the HPV target to the silica-redox dye reporter probe and capture probe, followed by electrochemical detection. The sensor was found to be highly specific and sensitive, with a detection limit of 22 fM for HPV-16 and 20 fM for HPV-18, between the range of 1 fM and 1 µM. Evaluation with oral and cervical samples showed that the biosensor result was consistent with the nested PCR/gel electrophoresis detection. The biosensor assay could be completed within 90 min. Due to its simplicity, rapidity, and high sensitivity, this biosensor could be used as an alternative method for HPV detection in clinical laboratories as well as for epidemiological studies.
</snippet>

Title: The Application of Functional Nanomaterials-Based Electrochemical Biosensors in Detecting Cancer Biomarkers: A Review
Snippet: Cervical cancer ranks among the most prevalent malignancies worldwide [114,115], with over half a million new diagnoses each year and more than 300,000 resulting deaths. Nearly all cases are attributed to high-risk strains of Human Papillomavirus (HPV), a disease that can largely be prevented. HPV-16 and HPV-18 account for 70% of cervical cancer cases worldwide. Together, eight specific types (HPV-16, HPV-18, HPV-33, HPV-45, HPV-31, HPV-58, HPV-52, and HPV-35) make up 90% of all cases [116]. In low-income countries, resource constraints often lead to a higher number of patients, as residents typically lack access to organized screening and HPV vaccination programs. Conversely, high-income countries typically offer more effective screening programs, resulting in a substantial decrease in the incidence and mortality rates of cervical cancer [117]. HPV E6/E7 mRNA detection offers greater specificity and positive predictive value in screening compared to HPV DNA detection. For example, Yang et al. [118] developed an electrochemical biosensor with a triple signal amplification strategy. This biosensor utilizes gold nanoparticles in conjunction with reverse transcription loop-mediated isothermal amplification and a high-affinity biotin-streptavidin system to detect HPV 16 E6/E7 mRNA (Figure 8a). Gold nanoparticles serve as carriers for functionalizing specific DNA probes, enabling efficient capture and enrichment of target RNA, thereby enhancing detection sensitivity and specificity. Achieving a detection limit of 0.08 fM (approximately 100 copies), it shows promising potential for clinical applications. Teengam et al. [119] designed a paper-based electrochemical biosensor capable of detecting HPV type 16 DNA using PCRamplified samples from the SiHa cell line (Figure 8b). This innovative sensor combines an anthraquinone-labeled pyrrolidinyl peptide nucleic acid probe with a graphene-polyanilinemodified electrode.
</snippet>

Snippet: Cervical cancer (CC) is the fourth most common cancer among women worldwide, following breast, colorectal, and lung cancers. However, treatment for metastatic cervical cancer is limited, with bevacizumab combined with chemotherapy being one of the few options, though survival rates remain low. Currently, the diagnosis of cervical cancer primarily relies on Pap smears and colposcopy. Although these methods are essential for detection, they are costly, labor-intensive, and require significant resources. Biomarker landscape for cervical cancer
Cervical cancer detection benefits from multiple biomarker modalities spanning viral nucleic acids (E6/E7 mRNA, HPV DNA), viral oncoproteins/antibodies, and host tumor proteins. <cite id="a951530b-0">Ultrasensitive ELISA quantification of HPV16 E7 oncoprotein in urine detected attomolar concentrations and discriminated oncogenic activity, revealing discrepancies versus E6/E7 PCR DNA presence, consistent with differences in viral life‑cycle and oncogenic activity</cite>. <cite id="a951530b-2">The ELISA distinguished specimens with low or no E7 from PCR‑positive ones, suggesting inactive infection; the assay related E7 levels to CIN grade and showed specificity for HPV16/related types over HPV18</cite>. <cite id="a951530b-1">A systematic review/meta‑analysis concluded that HPV16/18 E6/E7 antibodies show high specificity but suboptimal sensitivity for cervical cancer/CIN3 detection, supporting their utility as adjunct biomarkers but not as stand‑alone screening tools at present</cite>. <cite id="a951530b-3">HPV E6/E7 mRNA assays can outperform DNA genotyping for specificity and relate to lesion severity, yet E6/E7 mRNA positivity is lower in intraepithelial lesions and higher in carcinomas, implying value for triage and prognosis</cite>. <cite id="a951530b-4">A multiplex electrochemiluminescence immunoassay quantified type‑specific IgG to HPV16/18 E6 and E7, enabling analyte‑wise reference assignment and demonstrating assay specificity via competition/cross‑reactivity analyses</cite>.

Engineered filamentous phage nanofibers: materials, display, and design principles
Filamentous phage (e.g., M13/fd) provide biocompatible, high‑aspect‑ratio nanofibers that can be genetically programmed to display multiple targeting peptides and host affinity reagents or antigens. <cite id="c367735c-1">A dual‑display fd phage was engineered to present peptides that bind VEGF and PD‑L1; the nanofiber served as a capture reagent in ELISA and exhibited enhanced detection sensitivity versus single‑target antibody capture</cite>. <cite id="c367735c-2">In sandwich phage‑ELISA, phage nanoparticles at 50 μg/mL as coating showed positive serum rates of 78.9% for VEGF/sPD‑L1 versus 49.3% and 52.1% for single markers; AUCs improved from 0.756–0.778 to 0.896 when phage nanofibers were used as capture probes, with significantly higher sensitivity and specificity</cite>. <cite id="c367735c-3">Nanofiber architecture improves immobilization capacity and activity/stability of attached biomolecules, and fd phage nanofibers equipped with peptide fragments have been applied to cervical biomarker detection with higher sensitivity than conventional ELISA</cite>. <cite id="c367735c-4">Beyond peptide capture alone, combining phage nanofibers with co‑captured antigens (e.g., p53) synergistically increased detection rates and diagnostic accuracy in mixed cancer cohorts, illustrating modular “dual capture” engineering that can be transported to cervical markers</cite>.

Design takeaways include multivalency and orientation: multiple peptides can be arrayed along the nanofiber to increase local concentration and avidity, while the virus capsid provides structural context and stability. <cite id="c367735c-1">Dual peptide display on a single phage backbone enabled simultaneous recognition and binding of two biomarkers in one format, reducing assay complexity and enabling multiplexing</cite>. <cite id="c367735c-3">High surface area and loading capacity facilitate dense immobilization of capture elements or enzyme labels, improving signal and enabling integration with amplification strategies</cite>.

Title: Advanced detection of cervical cancer biomarkers using engineered filamentous phage nanofibers
Snippet: In the sandwich phage ELISA assay, phage nanoparticles at a concentration of 50 μg/mL were employed as the coating agent. A mixture of anti-VEGF and anti-PD-L1 antibodies served as the detection antibodies. The phage nanofibers detected VEGF and sPD-L1 in serum samples with a positive rate of 78.9%. Title: Nontoxic virus nanofibers improve the detection sensitivity for the anti-p53 antibody, a biomarker in cancer patients
Snippet: The presence of anti-p53 antibody in serum is a biomarker for cancer. However, its high sensitivity detection is still an issue in cancer diagnosis. To tackle this challenge, we used fd phage, a human-safe bacteria-specific virus nanofiber that can be mass-produced by infecting host bacteria in an error-free manner, and genetically engineered it to display a peptide capable of recognizing and capturing anti-p53 antibody on its side wall. We employed the resultant phage nanofibers as a capture probe to develop a modified version of the enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) method, termed phage-ELISA. We compared it to the traditional ELISA method for the detection of anti-p53 antibody, p53-ELISA, which uses recombinant wild-type p53 protein to capture anti-p53 antibody. We applied phage-ELISA to detect anti-p53 antibody in an experimental group of 316 patients with various types of malignant tumors. We found that a detection rate of 17.7% (56 positive cases) was achieved by phage-ELISA, which was comparable to the detection rate of 20.6% for p53-ELISA (65 positive cases). However, when both phage and p53 were combined to form antibody-capturing probes for phage/p53-ELISA, a detection rate of 30.4% (96 positive cases) was achieved. Our work showed that owing to the combined capture of the anti-p53 antibody by both phage nanofibers and p53, the phage/p53-ELISA achieved the highest diagnostic accuracy and detection efficiency for the anti-p53 antibody in patients with various types of cancers. Our work suggests that a combination of nanofibers and antigens, both of which capture antibody, could lead to increased detection sensitivity, which is useful for applications in the life sciences, clinical medicine, and environmental sciences.

Title: Portable, and ultrasensitive HR-HPV tests based on nucleic acid biosensors
Snippet: Cervical cancer is the third most common cancer threatening women’s health globally, and high-risk human papillomavirus (HR-HPV) infection is the main cause of cervical cancer worldwide. Given the recurrent nature of HR-HPV infection, accurate screening is essential for its control. Since the commonly used polymerase chain reaction (PCR) technique is limited by professional equipment and personnel, convenient and ultrasensitive detection methods for HR-HPV are still highly needed. As new molecular detection methods, nucleic acid amplification-based biosensors have the advantages of high sensitivity, rapid operation, and portability, which are helpful for point-of-care testing in rural and remote areas. This review summarized nucleic acid biosensors for HR-HPV screening based on a variety of nucleic acid amplification strategies involved in improved PCR, loop-mediated isothermal amplification, recombinase polymerase amplification, hybridization chain reaction, catalyzed hairpin assembly, and CRISPR/Cas systems. In combination with microfluidic technology, lateral flow assays, electrochemical analysis and other sensing technologies, HR-HPV nucleic acid biosensors have the advantages of high throughput, short response time, high sensitivity and easy operation in the field. Although there are still shortcomings, such as high cost and poor reproducibility, this approach will be suitable for on-site screening of HR-HPV infection or cervical cancer and for auxiliary clinical diagnosis in complex environments and poor areas in the future.

Title: Electrochemical Duplex Detection of E2 and E6 Genes of Human Papillomavirus Type 16 and Determination of Physical Status in High‐Risk Cervical Carcinoma
Snippet: Human papillomavirus type 16 (HPV‐16) is a key driver in the development of cervical carcinoma, with the integration of its genome into the host DNA marking a critical step in disease progression. Monitoring the physical state of HPV‐16, particularly the transition from episomal to integrated forms, is essential for evaluating the risk of malignancy development in cervix. This study presents the development of a duplex electrochemical biosensor for the simultaneous detection of the E2 and E6 genes of HPV‐16. Using a one‐step sandwich hybridization assay, the biosensor was able to detect HPV‐16 E2 and E6 genes with a sensitivity of 8 copies/mL and 12 copies/mL respectively and distinguish between the episomal and integrated forms based on the E2/E6 ratio (cut‐off 0.77, 100% sensitivity/specificity). The sensor was validated with 30 clinical cervical tissue samples, providing results comparable to qPCR method. This novel biosensor offers a rapid and efficient platform for the detection and monitoring of HPV‐16, with potential applications in cervical cancer screening and prognosis.

Title: A Multianalyte Electrochemical Genosensor for the Detection of High-Risk HPV Genotypes in Oral and Cervical Cancers
Snippet: Infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) is a major risk factor for oral and cervical cancers. Hence, we developed a multianalyte electrochemical DNA biosensor that could be used for both oral and cervical samples to detect the high-risk HPV genotypes 16 and 18. The assay involves the sandwich hybridization of the HPV target to the silica-redox dye reporter probe and capture probe, followed by electrochemical detection. The sensor was found to be highly specific and sensitive, with a detection limit of 22 fM for HPV-16 and 20 fM for HPV-18, between the range of 1 fM and 1 µM. Evaluation with oral and cervical samples showed that the biosensor result was consistent with the nested PCR/gel electrophoresis detection. The biosensor assay could be completed within 90 min. Due to its simplicity, rapidity, and high sensitivity, this biosensor could be used as an alternative method for HPV detection in clinical laboratories as well as for epidemiological studies.

Title: The Application of Functional Nanomaterials-Based Electrochemical Biosensors in Detecting Cancer Biomarkers: A Review
Snippet: Cervical cancer ranks among the most prevalent malignancies worldwide [114,115], with over half a million new diagnoses each year and more than 300,000 resulting deaths. Nearly all cases are attributed to high-risk strains of Human Papillomavirus (HPV), a disease that can largely be prevented. HPV-16 and HPV-18 account for 70% of cervical cancer cases worldwide. Together, eight specific types (HPV-16, HPV-18, HPV-33, HPV-45, HPV-31, HPV-58, HPV-52, and HPV-35) make up 90% of all cases [116]. In low-income countries, resource constraints often lead to a higher number of patients, as residents typically lack access to organized screening and HPV vaccination programs. Conversely, high-income countries typically offer more effective screening programs, resulting in a substantial decrease in the incidence and mortality rates of cervical cancer [117]. HPV E6/E7 mRNA detection offers greater specificity and positive predictive value in screening compared to HPV DNA detection. For example, Yang et al. [118] developed an electrochemical biosensor with a triple signal amplification strategy. This biosensor utilizes gold nanoparticles in conjunction with reverse transcription loop-mediated isothermal amplification and a high-affinity biotin-streptavidin system to detect HPV 16 E6/E7 mRNA (Figure 8a). Gold nanoparticles serve as carriers for functionalizing specific DNA probes, enabling efficient capture and enrichment of target RNA, thereby enhancing detection sensitivity and specificity. Achieving a detection limit of 0.08 fM (approximately 100 copies), it shows promising potential for clinical applications. Teengam et al. [119] designed a paper-based electrochemical biosensor capable of detecting HPV type 16 DNA using PCRamplified samples from the SiHa cell line (Figure 8b). This innovative sensor combines an anthraquinone-labeled pyrrolidinyl peptide nucleic acid probe with a graphene-polyanilinemodified electrode.

Snippet: Cervical cancer (CC) is the fourth most common cancer among women worldwide, following breast, colorectal, and lung cancers. Each year, it accounts for approximately 600,000 new cases and 340,000 deaths. Early-stage cervical cancer is treatable with surgery and chemoradiotherapy (CCRT). However, treatment for metastatic cervical cancer is limited, with bevacizumab combined with chemotherapy being one of the few options, though survival rates remain low. Currently, the diagnosis of cervical cancer primarily relies on Pap smears and colposcopy. Although these methods are essential for detection, they are costly, labor-intensive, and require significant resources. Therefore, there is an urgent need to identify effective biomarkers that can detect cervical cancer at an early stage, improving both the accuracy of diagnosis and the efficacy of treatment. Furthermore, we discussed the limitations and future prospects of electrochemical biosensors in this field.

documents.title: Portable, and ultrasensitive HR-HPV tests based on nucleic acid biosensors
documents.snippet: Cervical cancer is the third most common cancer threatening women’s health globally, and high-risk human papillomavirus (HR-HPV) infection is the main cause of cervical cancer worldwide. Given the recurrent nature of HR-HPV infection, accurate screening is essential for its control. Since the commonly used polymerase chain reaction (PCR) technique is limited by professional equipment and personnel, convenient and ultrasensitive detection methods for HR-HPV are still highly needed. As new molecular detection methods, nucleic acid amplification-based biosensors have the advantages of high sensitivity, rapid operation, and portability, which are helpful for point-of-care testing in rural and remote areas. This review summarized nucleic acid biosensors for HR-HPV screening based on a variety of nucleic acid amplification strategies involved in improved PCR, loop-mediated isothermal amplification, recombinase polymerase amplification, hybridization chain reaction, catalyzed hairpin assembly, and CRISPR/Cas systems. In combination with microfluidic technology, lateral flow assays, electrochemical analysis and other sensing technologies, HR-HPV nucleic acid biosensors have the advantages of high throughput, short response time, high sensitivity and easy operation in the field. Although there are still shortcomings, such as high cost and poor reproducibility, this approach will be suitable for on-site screening of HR-HPV infection or cervical cancer and for auxiliary clinical diagnosis in complex environments and poor areas in the future.

documents.title: Electrochemical Duplex Detection of E2 and E6 Genes of Human Papillomavirus Type 16 and Determination of Physical Status in High‐Risk Cervical Carcinoma
documents.snippet: Human papillomavirus type 16 (HPV‐16) is a key driver in the development of cervical carcinoma, with the integration of its genome into the host DNA marking a critical step in disease progression. Monitoring the physical state of HPV‐16, particularly the transition from episomal to integrated forms, is essential for evaluating the risk of malignancy development in cervix. This study presents the development of a duplex electrochemical biosensor for the simultaneous detection of the E2 and E6 genes of HPV‐16. Using a one‐step sandwich hybridization assay, the biosensor was able to detect HPV‐16 E2 and E6 genes with a sensitivity of 8 copies/mL and 12 copies/mL respectively and distinguish between the episomal and integrated forms based on the E2/E6 ratio (cut‐off 0.77, 100% sensitivity/specificity). The sensor was validated with 30 clinical cervical tissue samples, providing results comparable to qPCR method. This novel biosensor offers a rapid and efficient platform for the detection and monitoring of HPV‐16, with potential applications in cervical cancer screening and prognosis.

documents.title: A Multianalyte Electrochemical Genosensor for the Detection of High-Risk HPV Genotypes in Oral and Cervical Cancers
documents.snippet: Infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) is a major risk factor for oral and cervical cancers. Hence, we developed a multianalyte electrochemical DNA biosensor that could be used for both oral and cervical samples to detect the high-risk HPV genotypes 16 and 18. The assay involves the sandwich hybridization of the HPV target to the silica-redox dye reporter probe and capture probe, followed by electrochemical detection. The sensor was found to be highly specific and sensitive, with a detection limit of 22 fM for HPV-16 and 20 fM for HPV-18, between the range of 1 fM and 1 µM. Evaluation with oral and cervical samples showed that the biosensor result was consistent with the nested PCR/gel electrophoresis detection. The biosensor assay could be completed within 90 min. Due to its simplicity, rapidity, and high sensitivity, this biosensor could be used as an alternative method for HPV detection in clinical laboratories as well as for epidemiological studies.
